problems.title: Binary Search
problems.statement:
Given an array of integers `nums` which is sorted in ascending order, and an integer `target`, write a function to search `target` in `nums`. If `target` exists, then return its index. Otherwise, return `-1`.

You must write an algorithm with `O(log n)` runtime complexity.
constraints: All the integers in nums are unique.
nums is sorted in ascending order.

examples.explanation: 9 exists in nums and its index is 4.
Edge/boundary case for Binary Search testing minimal, empty, or single-element inputs.

commonMistakes: Using (left + right) / 2 which can overflow 32-bit signed integer in other languages
Using left < right instead of left <= right
hints: Since the array is sorted, compare target against the midpoint.
Calculate mid using left + Math.floor((right - left) / 2).
If nums[mid] === target return mid; narrow bounds accordingly.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=5000 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=5000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Search Insert Position
problems.statement:
Given a sorted array of distinct integers and a target value, return the index if the target is found. If not, return the index where it would be if it were inserted in order.

You must write an algorithm with `O(log n)` runtime complexity.
constraints: nums contains distinct values sorted in ascending order.
commonMistakes: Returning mid or right instead of left when target is not found
hints: Binary search for the target.
When the loop terminates (left > right), `left` is the exact lower bound index where target should be inserted.

problems.title: First Bad Version
problems.statement:
You are a product manager and currently leading a team to develop a new product. Unfortunately, the latest version of your product fails the quality check. Since each version is developed based on the previous version, all the versions after a bad version are also bad.

Suppose you have `n` versions `[1, 2, ..., n]` and you want to find out the first bad one, which causes all the following ones to be bad.

Given `n` and an API `isBadVersion(version)` (or simulate by providing bad version `bad`), return the first bad version.

examples.explanation: Version 4 is the first bad version.
Version 1 is the first bad version.
Edge/boundary case for First Bad Version testing minimal, empty, or single-element inputs.

commonMistakes: Setting right = mid - 1 when mid is bad (mid itself could be the FIRST bad version)
hints: If mid is bad, the first bad version must be at mid or to the left: right = mid.
If mid is good, the first bad version must be strictly to the right: left = mid + 1.
Terminate when left === right.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Guess Number Higher or Lower
problems.statement:
We are playing the Guess Game. The game is as follows:

I pick a number from `1` to `n`. You have to guess which number I picked.

Every time you guess wrong, I will tell you whether the number I picked is higher or lower than your guess.

Return the number that I picked.
commonMistakes: Integer overflow when calculating (left + right) / 2
hints: Binary search between 1 and n.
If mid < pick, search right half: left = mid + 1.
If mid > pick, search left half: right = mid - 1.

problems.title: Sqrt(x)
problems.statement:
Given a non-negative integer `x`, return the square root of `x` rounded down to the nearest integer. The returned integer should be non-negative as well.

You must not use any built-in exponent function or operator, such as `pow(x, 0.5)` or `x ** 0.5`.

examples.explanation: Edge/boundary case for Sqrt(x) testing minimal, empty, or single-element inputs.

commonMistakes: Using built-in Math.sqrt (disallowed)
Overflow on mid * mid
hints: Binary search in range [1, x / 2].
If mid * mid <= x, record mid as potential answer and try larger values.
Otherwise try smaller values.

problems.title: Valid Perfect Square
problems.statement:
Given a positive integer `num`, return `true` if `num` is a perfect square or `false` otherwise.

A perfect square is an integer that is the square of an integer. In other words, it is the product of some integer with itself.

You must not use any built-in library function, such as `sqrt`.

examples.explanation: Edge/boundary case for Valid Perfect Square testing minimal, empty, or single-element inputs.

commonMistakes: Linear scanning causing TLE on 2^31 - 1
hints: Binary search for integer x such that x * x == num.
Search range [1, num].

problems.title: Find Smallest Letter Greater Than Target
problems.statement:
You are given an array of characters `letters` that is sorted in non-decreasing order, and a character `target`. There are at least two different characters in `letters`.

Return the smallest character in `letters` that is lexicographically greater than `target`. If such a character does not exist, return the first character in `letters`.
constraints: letters[i] is a lowercase English letter.
letters is sorted in non-decreasing order.
target is a lowercase English letter.
commonMistakes: Failing to wrap around to letters[0] when target is >= all characters
hints: Find the first letter strictly greater than target.
If letters[mid] <= target, search right: left = mid + 1.
Wrap around using left % letters.length.

problems.title: Search a 2D Matrix
problems.statement:
You are given an `m x n` integer matrix `matrix` with the following two properties:
- Each row is sorted in non-decreasing order.
- The first integer of each row is greater than the last integer of the previous row.

Given an integer `target`, return `true` if `target` is in `matrix` or `false` otherwise.

You must write a solution in `O(log(m * n))` time complexity.

examples.explanation: Edge/boundary case for Search a 2D Matrix testing minimal, empty, or single-element inputs.

commonMistakes: Converting index to 2D coordinates: row = Math.floor(mid / n), col = mid % n (using m instead of n causes indexing errors)
hints: The entire matrix behaves like a single sorted 1D array of length m * n.
Perform binary search on virtual 1D array from 0 to m * n - 1.
Map mid to (row, col) via row = Math.floor(mid / n), col = mid % n.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=50 for complexity verification

problems.title: Find First and Last Position of Element in Sorted Array
problems.statement:
Given an array of integers `nums` sorted in non-decreasing order, find the starting and ending position of a given `target` value.

If `target` is not found in the array, return `[-1, -1]`.

You must write an algorithm with `O(log n)` runtime complexity.
constraints: nums is sorted in non-decreasing order.
commonMistakes: Finding target once and expanding linearly left and right O(N) when all elements are duplicates
hints: Run two binary searches: one for the first occurrence, one for the last.
To find the first occurrence, when nums[mid] === target, continue searching left: right = mid - 1.
To find the last occurrence, when nums[mid] === target, continue searching right: left = mid + 1.

problems.title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array
problems.statement:
Suppose an array of length `n` sorted in ascending order is rotated between 1 and `n` times.

Given the sorted rotated array `nums` of unique elements, return the minimum element of this array.

You must write an algorithm that runs in `O(log n)` time.

parameterDefinitions.name: nums
parameterDefinitions.description: Rotated sorted array of unique elements

constraints: All the integers of nums are unique.
commonMistakes: Comparing nums[mid] with nums[left] instead of nums[right]
hints: Compare nums[mid] with nums[right].
If nums[mid] > nums[right], the inflection point (minimum) must lie strictly to the right: left = mid + 1.
If nums[mid] <= nums[right], the minimum is at mid or to the left: right = mid.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=3000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
problems.statement:
There is an integer array `nums` sorted in ascending order (with distinct values).

Prior to being passed to your function, `nums` is possibly rotated at an unknown pivot index.

Given the array `nums` after the possible rotation and an integer `target`, return the index of `target` if it is in `nums`, or `-1` if it is not in `nums`.

You must write an algorithm with `O(log n)` runtime complexity.
constraints: All values of nums are unique.
nums is an ascending array that is possibly rotated.
commonMistakes: Failing to determine which half is sorted before comparing target with bounds
hints: At least one half of [left..right] is always normally sorted.
If nums[left] <= nums[mid], the left half is sorted. Check if target lies within [nums[left], nums[mid]).
Otherwise the right half is sorted. Check if target lies within (nums[mid], nums[right]].

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=3000 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=4000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array II
problems.statement:
There is an integer array `nums` sorted in non-decreasing order (not necessarily with distinct values).

Before being passed to your function, `nums` is rotated at an unknown pivot index.

Given the array `nums` after rotation and an integer `target`, return `true` if `target` is in `nums`, or `false` if it is not in `nums`.

You must decrease the overall operation steps as much as possible.

parameterDefinitions.name: nums
parameterDefinitions.description: Rotated sorted array with potential duplicates

constraints: nums is guaranteed to be rotated at some pivot.

examples.explanation: Edge/boundary case for Search in Rotated Sorted Array II testing minimal, empty, or single-element inputs.

problems.optimalTimeComplexity: O(log N) average, O(N) worst case with all duplicates
commonMistakes: Infinite loop when nums[left] === nums[mid] === nums[right]
hints: Duplicates introduce ambiguity: if nums[left] === nums[mid] === nums[right], we cannot deduce which half is sorted.
In that case, simply increment left and decrement right.
Otherwise proceed with standard rotated binary search.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=3001 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=3000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Find Peak Element
problems.statement:
A peak element is an element that is strictly greater than its neighbors.

Given a 0-indexed integer array `nums`, find a peak element, and return its index. If the array contains multiple peaks, return the index to any of the peaks.

You may imagine that `nums[-1] = nums[n] = -infinity`.

You must write an algorithm that runs in `O(log n)` time.
constraints: nums[i] != nums[i + 1] for all valid i.

examples.explanation: 3 is a peak element and its index is 2.
Edge/boundary case for Find Peak Element testing minimal, empty, or single-element inputs.

commonMistakes: Linear scanning O(N) instead of binary searching the slope O(log N)
hints: If nums[mid] > nums[mid + 1], you are on a downward slope, so a peak must exist to the left (including mid): right = mid.
If nums[mid] < nums[mid + 1], you are on an upward slope, so a peak must exist to the right: left = mid + 1.

problems.title: Peak Index in a Mountain Array
problems.statement:
An array `arr` is a mountain if the following properties hold:
- `arr.length >= 3`
- There exists some `i` with `0 < i < arr.length - 1` such that:
  - `arr[0] < arr[1] < ... < arr[i - 1] < arr[i]`
  - `arr[i] > arr[i + 1] > ... > arr[arr.length - 1]`

Given a mountain array `arr`, return the index `i` such that `arr[0] < arr[1] < ... < arr[i - 1] < arr[i] > arr[i + 1] > ... > arr[arr.length - 1]`.

You must solve it in `O(log(arr.length))` time complexity.
constraints: arr is guaranteed to be a mountain array.
commonMistakes: Linear scanning O(N)
hints: Binary search for the inflection where arr[mid] > arr[mid + 1].
If arr[mid] < arr[mid + 1], peak is to the right: left = mid + 1.
Otherwise peak is at mid or left: right = mid.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=3000 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=4000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Single Element in a Sorted Array
problems.statement:
You are given a sorted array consisting of only integers where every element appears exactly twice, except for one element which appears exactly once.

Return the single element that appears only once.

Your solution must run in `O(log n)` time and `O(1)` space.

parameterDefinitions.name: nums
parameterDefinitions.description: Sorted array of pairs and one single

examples.explanation: Edge/boundary case for Single Element in a Sorted Array testing minimal, empty, or single-element inputs.

commonMistakes: Using XOR which runs in O(N) rather than the required O(log N)
hints: Before the single element, pairs start on even indices (0, 2, 4, ...).
After the single element, pairs start on odd indices.
Ensure mid is even (if mid is odd, decrement by 1).
If nums[mid] === nums[mid + 1], single is to the right: left = mid + 2; else right = mid.

Stress test scale N=4001 for complexity verification

problems.title: Kth Missing Positive Number
problems.statement:
Given an array `arr` of positive integers sorted in a strictly increasing order, and an integer `k`.

Return the `k`th positive integer that is missing from this array.
constraints: arr[i] < arr[j] for 1 <= i < j <= arr.length

examples.explanation: Edge/boundary case for Kth Missing Positive Number testing minimal, empty, or single-element inputs.

hints: At index mid, the number of missing positive integers before arr[mid] is arr[mid] - (mid + 1).
Binary search for the first index where missing >= k.
The answer is left + k.

problems.title: Arranging Coins
problems.statement:
You have `n` coins and you want to build a staircase with these coins. The staircase consists of `k` rows where the `i`th row has exactly `i` coins. The last row of the staircase may be incomplete.

Given the integer `n`, return the number of complete rows of the staircase you will build.

examples.explanation: Row 1 (1), Row 2 (2). Row 3 has 2 coins < 3, so 2 complete rows.
Row 1 (1), Row 2 (2), Row 3 (3). Row 4 incomplete (2 < 4), so 3 complete rows.
Edge/boundary case for Arranging Coins testing minimal, empty, or single-element inputs.

commonMistakes: Subtracting coins iteratively leading to TLE on 2^31 - 1
hints: A staircase of k rows requires k * (k + 1) / 2 coins.
Binary search for the maximum k such that k * (k + 1) / 2 <= n.

problems.title: Heaters
problems.statement:
Winter is coming! During the contest, your first job is to design a standard heater with a fixed warm radius to warm all the houses.

Every house can be warmed, as long as the house is within the heater's warm radius range.

Given the positions of `houses` and `heaters` on a horizontal line, return the minimum radius standard of heaters so that all houses could be covered by those heaters.

examples.explanation: Heater at 2 covers 1 and 3 with radius 1.
Heater at 2 needs radius 3 to reach 5.

problems.optimalTimeComplexity: O(N log M + M log M)
commonMistakes: Checking only the closest heater to the right and forgetting the closest heater to the left
hints: Sort heaters.
For each house, binary search in heaters to find the closest heater to the left and closest heater to the right.
The minimum distance to heat this house is min(distLeft, distRight).
The answer is the maximum over all houses.

problems.title: Successful Pairs of Spells and Potions
problems.statement:
You are given two positive integer arrays `spells` and `potions`, of length `n` and `m` respectively, where `spells[i]` represents the strength of the `i`th spell and `potions[j]` represents the strength of the `j`th potion.

You are also given an integer `success`. A spell and potion pair is considered successful if the product of their strengths is at least `success`.

Return an integer array `pairs` of length `n` where `pairs[i]` is the number of potions that will form a successful pair with the `i`th spell.

examples.explanation: Spell 5 needs >= 1.4 -> 4 potions. Spell 1 needs >= 7 -> 0. Spell 3 needs >= 2.33 -> 3 potions.
Edge/boundary case for Successful Pairs of Spells and Potions testing minimal, empty, or single-element inputs.

problems.optimalTimeComplexity: O(M log M + N log M)
commonMistakes: Nested loops O(N * M) causing TLE
Integer overflow when computing s * p in 32-bit environments
hints: Sort potions array.
For each spell, calculate minimum required potion strength = Math.ceil(success / spell).
Use binary search (lower bound) in potions to find the first potion meeting the requirement.

Stress test scale N=3000 for complexity verification

Return `x` if the array is special, or `-1` otherwise. It can be proven that if `nums` is special, the value for `x` is unique.

hints: x must be between 1 and nums.length.
Sort nums and check candidate x values using binary search or counting.

problems.title: Find the Distance Value Between Two Arrays
problems.statement:
Given two integer arrays `arr1` and `arr2`, and the integer `d`, return the distance value between the two arrays.

The distance value is defined as the number of elements `arr1[i]` such that there is not any element `arr2[j]` where `|arr1[i] - arr2[j]| <= d`.

examples.explanation: 4 and 5 have no element in arr2 with abs diff <= 2.
Edge/boundary case for Find the Distance Value Between Two Arrays testing minimal, empty, or single-element inputs.

problems.optimalTimeComplexity: O(N log M + M log M)
commonMistakes: Failing to break early when |arr2[mid] - val| <= d is satisfied
hints: Sort arr2.
For each element in arr1, binary search in arr2 for any element in [val - d, val + d].
If none exists, increment result count.

A conveyor belt has packages that must be shipped from one port to another within `days` days.

The `i`th package on the conveyor belt has a weight of `weights[i]`. Each day, we load the ship with packages on the conveyor belt (in the order given by `weights`). We may not load more weight than the maximum weight capacity of the ship.

Return the least weight capacity of the ship that will result in all the packages on the conveyor belt being shipped within `days` days.
commonMistakes: Setting lower search bound to 1 instead of Math.max(...weights) (the ship must carry at least the heaviest single item)
hints: Search on the answer: capacity must be in [max(weights), sum(weights)].
Check if capacity C is feasible in O(N).
If feasible, try smaller capacity: right = mid. Otherwise left = mid + 1.

problems.title: Koko Eating Bananas
problems.statement:
Koko loves to eat bananas. There are `n` piles of bananas, the `i`th pile has `piles[i]` bananas. The guards have gone and will come back in `h` hours.

Koko can decide her bananas-per-hour eating speed of `k`. Each hour, she chooses some pile of bananas and eats `k` bananas from that pile. If the pile has less than `k` bananas, she eats all of them instead and will not eat any more bananas during this hour.

Koko likes to eat slowly but still wants to finish eating all the bananas before the guards return.

Return the minimum integer `k` such that she can eat all the bananas within `h` hours.

examples.explanation: At speed 4, Koko finishes in 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 = 8 hours.
At speed 30, Koko finishes in 5 hours.
At speed 23, Koko finishes in 6 hours.

commonMistakes: Math.ceil precision issues with large floats in JavaScript (p / speed)
hints: Binary search on speed k in range [1, max(piles)].
Hours needed for pile p at speed k is Math.ceil(p / k) = Math.floor((p + k - 1) / k).
If total hours <= h, k is feasible; try smaller: right = mid.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=3000 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=4000 for complexity verification
